Not sure if anyone else has noticed, but almost every large finance YouTube channel seems to be calling AI a bubble and comparing it to the dot-com era.

To me, that just highlights the disconnect.

A lot of people (including these YouTubers) missed one of the biggest wealth creation opportunities of the decade, and now every pullback becomes proof that the entire thing is a bubble.

Now, don't get me wrong.

There are definitely companies trading at ridiculous valuations today, and plenty of low-quality names have been dragged higher by the AI narrative.

But lumping everything together and calling it "the dot-com bubble" misses the point.

Companies like $NVDA and $MU aren't selling dreams.

They're selling products into real demand, generating real revenue, and struggling to keep up with customer orders.

That's fundamentally different from companies that had no business model, no profits, and often no real product.

Could there be corrections? Absolutely.

Could some AI stocks fall 50%? Of course.

But comparing today's AI infrastructure leaders to "Pets. com" simply ignores the reality of what's happening on the ground.

The demand is real.
The spending is real.
The revenue is real.

And in my opinion, we're still much earlier than most people think, despite the recent run up, new highs will be made, even if a huge correction occurs.

I have a gamer background, and I treat the stock market like a game.

The goal isn’t to win every trade.
The goal is to maximize win rate + asymmetric upside.
My first-glance framework for stock picking:

1. Is the sector growing?
 example for sectors: AI apps, memory, EVs, business software, etc.

If the industry itself isn’t growing, I usually stop researching immediately.

2. Is the company revenue EXPECTED to grow / accelerate?
 Past growth can be misleading.

 Future demand is what matters:

• customer mapping
• demand trends
• product positioning
• sector tailwinds
 If future growth isn’t there, I move on.

3. Founder-led with skin in the game?
 Not mandatory, but one of my strongest signals.
 Founders whose wealth is tied to the company usually think long term and act like owners.

 That mindset helped me get into $TSLA, $SE, and $NET very early.

4. Margin expansion potential or very steady high margin.

 One of the clearest signs of strength.

 When a company gains pricing power → margins expand.
 And sustained margin expansion usually means there’s a moat underneath.

 This point is usually a must too(unless there's a clear explanation on why it's dropping)

This framework massively reduced the amount of garbage I research.

For some companies it'd be harder to find some of the data or infer, so I usually don't take the risk as I like favourable risk reward ratios.

These are the first things I look at before I even start a deep dive that you can apply today on your companies and see how they're positioned win-rate wise.
